title: Off-Policy Merging Beats On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Learning

paper.title: Off-Policy Merging Beats On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract A long-standing goal of AI is a model that can continually learn and improve itself. On post-trained models, supervised finetuning (SFT) on new data often causes poor generalization and catastrophic forgetting. As such, the conventional wisdom is that on-policy training is a prerequisite for continual learning. In practice, however, data containing new knowledge or capabilities are often off-policy . While methods such as on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) try to bridge this gap by converting off-policy data into on-policy signal, they have been shown to cause reasoning collapse.
In this paper, we show that off-policy merging beats OPSD for continual learning .
We first show that SFT learns a useful signal from new data, but naively applying its update interferes with existing capabilities. We reduce this interference with a simple recipe we term grafting , which changes where the update is learned and how it is applied: (1) learning the update on an earlier donor checkpoint , ideally even before the end of pretraining , and applying the weight update to the post-trained model; (2) scaling the weight update, equivalent to a form of model merging; and (3) optionally, masking the most sensitive update directions when the new data distribution is far from the post-trained model. Across continual learning settings including (1) distilling from expert traces, (2) self-improvement with STaR and Pedagogical RL, and (3) injecting knowledge after pretraining cutoff, grafting Pareto-dominates both SFT and OPSD in new-task and old-task performance, while avoiding expensive on-policy sampling. Therefore, our work challenges on-policy training as a necessity for continual learning on RL-trained models.

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: A long-standing goal of AI is a model that keeps acquiring new capabilities without forgetting what it can already do ( McCloskey and Cohen, 1989 ; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ) . This is particularly challenging for models that have undergone extensive post-training. In particular, direct supervised finetuning (SFT) on new data can cause forgetting and fail to generalize ( Chu et al., 2025 ) . This has motivated the view that continual learning should remain on-policy , i.e. the model learns from behavior produced by its current policy ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . However, extended on-policy RL can plateau and lose coverage after exhausting non-zero reward behaviors to amplify ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Furthermore, data containing new knowledge or capabilities are often off-policy , such as new knowledge after the pretraining cutoff Jang et al. (2022) , expert demonstrations Taori et al. (2023) , delayed feedback from environments Trajectory Labs (2026) , and synthetic data for self-improvement Chakraborty et al. (2026) . Recent work on on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) tries to bridge this gap by converting off-policy data into on-policy updates, distilling from a solution-conditioned copy of the model ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hubotter et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . However, conditioning on the solution can suppress exploration, leak privileged information into the teacher’s reasoning, and degrade out-of-domain performance or collapse reasoning length ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Kaur et al., 2026 ) . More fundamentally, this raises a simple question: Is on-policy training necessary for continual learning, or are we using off-policy updates poorly? We premise with a surprisingly simple finding: model merging, i.e., by interpolating the SFT-ed weights back toward the original post-trained model Wortsman et al. (2022b) , θ merge = ( 1 − λ ) ​ θ post + λ ​ θ post ′ \theta_{\text{merge}}=(1-\lambda)\,\theta_{\text{post}}+\lambda\,\theta_{\text{post}}^{\prime} where θ post ′ \theta_{\text{post}}^{\prime} is the model after SFT on a task, SFT is elevated to a strong baseline (Figure 1 , left), achieving higher performance on the new task and comparable performance on old tasks. Since merging only scales the SFT update down without changing its direction, this demonstrates SFT learns a useful signal from the new data. However, naive integration of SFT updates clearly interferes with the post-trained model’s capabilities. This leads to a tangible key objective: Figure 1: (Left) Model merging alone greatly improve generalization; Grafting dominates SFT and OPSD. Model: Qwen3-1.7B (thinking). (Right) The best donor model for grafting is even before the end of pretraining . Model: OLMo-3-7B (thinking). Only frontier points are plotted. How can we better minimize the interference induced by off-policy updates? We first rewrite merging as adding a scaled update to the post-trained model, θ merge = θ post + λ ⁡ ( θ post ′ − θ post ) \theta_{\text{merge}}=\theta_{\text{post}}+\lambda\,({\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}\theta_{\text{post}}^{\prime}}-{\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}\theta_{\text{post}}}) . Written this way, merging decouples two design choices: where the update is learned (here, naively on θ post \theta_{\text{post}} itself) and how it is applied (here, naively scaled by λ \lambda ). Task arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) shows that an update need not be derived from the model it is applied to. We argue that this separation is important for continual learning. This is because training on a narrow distribution skews which task a model infers its inputs to come from ( Kotha et al., 2024 ) , so finetuning the post-trained model routes much of the new learning signal through the parameters supporting its existing capabilities, while a checkpoint from before post-training routes less of it there (§ 3 ). We therefore learn the update on an earlier donor model θ donor {\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}\theta_{\text{donor}}} , and apply it to the post-trained model: θ post + λ ⁡ ( θ donor-ft − θ donor ) \theta_{\text{post}}+\lambda\,({\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}\theta_{\text{donor-ft}}}-{\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}\theta_{\text{donor}}}) , where θ donor-ft \theta_{\text{donor-ft}} is the donor after finetuning. Along the OLMo-3 training trajectory ( OLMo Team, 2026 ) , we see that the best donors are checkpoints before the end of pretraining (Figure 1 , right), which is perhaps not surprising since later stages of modern pretraining are high-quality data that resembles post-training. Donor-trained updates with naive scaling write less to the parameters on which the post-trained model is most sensitive, but when the new distribution is far from the post-trained model, they can still damage them. We therefore propose to optionally protect the most sensitive directions, estimated with the Fisher information ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Ikram et al., 2026 ) . This matters most for knowledge injection (§ 6.2 ), where retaining unrelated capabilities is hard. We call the full recipe grafting : θ post + λ ⋅ ℳ ρ ​ ( θ donor-ft − θ donor ) \theta_{\text{post}}+\lambda\cdot{\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.6836,0.375}\mathcal{M}_{\rho}}({\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}\theta_{\text{donor-ft}}}-{\color[rgb]{0.1602,0.5,0.7266}\theta_{\text{donor}}}) , where the mask ℳ ρ {\color[rgb]{0.1523,0.6836,0.375}\mathcal{M}_{\rho}} projects away the top- ρ \rho fraction of Fisher-weighted directions from the update. We study three settings where off-policy data arises naturally: (1) distillation from expert traces on hard problems the model cannot solve; (2) self-improvement on hard problems, where models bootstrap themselves without stronger supervision, e.g., via their own rejection-sampled successes ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) or with indirect supervision, e.g., from thinking traces written by a copy of themselves with privileged information ( Chakraborty et al., 2026 , Pedagogical RL;) , and (3) knowledge injection of new facts absent from prior training. In all three, we assume access only to the data (with our without thinking traces depending on the specific setting), not to the weights or logits of a stronger teacher model, so on-policy distillation (OPD) from a teacher ( Agarwal et al., 2023 ) is not possible. In all three settings, grafting dominates OPSD in both new-task and old-task performance while avoiding expensive on-policy sampling. In self-improvement, grafting roughly doubles new-task performance over the post-trained model while also improving old-task performance. Together, our results suggest that on-policy updates are not a necessary condition for continual learning. Since continual learning applications often involve off-policy experiences, we hope our work inspires more effort on making off-policy training generalize.

sections.heading: 2  Preliminaries
sections.text: We consider teaching a post-trained model π θ post \pi_{\theta_{\text{post}}} a new target task, formally a set of inputs { x } \{x\} which we want the model to solve. A task may be a skill (e.g., a class of hard math problems) or some knowledge (e.g., new facts after the knowledge cutoff). Two objectives should be optimized jointly: • New task : performance on held-out IID instances of the target task. • Old task : performance on tasks outside the target task – for unrelated tasks, we want less forgetting; for related tasks, we want the new skill or knowledge to generalize to these tasks. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a standard way to learn a task without using off-policy data. It maximizes 𝔼 y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) R ( x , y ) \mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\,R(x,y) over outputs it samples itself. However, given its mode-seeking nature, RL is known to mostly amplify and compose behaviors the model already possesses ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . For genuinely new knowledge or very hard problems beyond the model’s capability, the model places almost no probability on correct outputs and, therefore, receives no training signal to continue improving. These are the scenarios where off-policy data can be extremely useful. Off-policy data can be formalized as a corpus 𝒟 = { ( x , y ) } \mathcal{D}=\{(x,y)\} of inputs x x and outputs y y , where x x are not generated under π θ post \pi_{\theta_{\text{post}}} . Such data is abundant in practice, e.g., new knowledge acquired after the model’s pretraining cutoff, expert demonstrations for a hard task, feedback from new environments, and synthetic data created by the model for self-improvement. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has been the standard way to learn from off-policy data, optimizing the model likelihood − 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ 𝒟 ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( y ∣ x ) -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) directly on the outputs y y given by the data 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . However, SFT is known to memorize rather than generalize ( Chu et al., 2025 ) and to cause catastrophic forgetting of capabilities outside 𝒟 \mathcal{D} ( McCloskey and Cohen, 1989 ; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ; Biderman et al., 2024 ) . On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) addresses the shortcomings of SFT by converting the off-policy corpus into on-policy updates ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hubotter et al., 2026 ) . The model samples responses and is supervised at each token by a solution-conditioned version of itself: 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ 𝒟 𝔼 y ~ ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y ) ∑ t D α ( π θ ¯ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y , y ~ < t ) ∥ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y ~ < t ) ) , \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{y}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\,y)}\,\sum_{t}\mathrm{D}_{\alpha}\!\big(\pi_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,y,\tilde{y}_{<t})\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\tilde{y}_{<t})\big), where the teacher θ ¯ \bar{\theta} is a stop-grad copy of the student , and D α \mathrm{D}_{\alpha} is a family of f f -divergences ( Agarwal et al., 2023 ) whose α \alpha interpolates from forward KL ( α = 0 \alpha{=}0 ) to reverse KL ( α = 1 \alpha{=}1 ).

We display the core recipe in Algorithm 1 . Extract updates from a donor model Task arithmetic ( Ilharco et al., 2023 ) shows that an update need not be derived from the model it is applied to. We argue that this separation is important for continual learning. This is because training on a narrow distribution skews which task a model infers its inputs to come from ( Kotha et al., 2024 ) , so finetuning the post-trained model routes much of the new learning signal through the parameters supporting its existing capabilities, while a checkpoint from before post-training routes less of it there (§ 3 ). Therefore, instead of directly finetuning the post-trained model θ post \theta_{\text{post}} , we finetune an earlier checkpoint which we call a “donor model” θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} . Specifically, we finetune θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} to obtain θ donor-ft \theta_{\text{donor-ft}} , and isolate the difference Δ = θ donor-ft − θ donor \Delta=\theta_{\text{donor-ft}}-\theta_{\text{donor}} . sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: Models We experiment with two model pairs: Qwen3-1.7B (thinking) / Qwen3-1.7B-Base Yang et al. (2025) and Qwen3-8B (thinking) / Qwen3-8B-Base as the post-trained model θ post \theta_{\text{post}} and the donor model θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} . Our experiments include both thinking and instruct modes. Unless stated otherwise the donor model is the officially released base model of the same family. In § 5.3 we additionally use OLMo-3-7B (thinking) ( OLMo Team, 2026 ) as θ post \theta_{\text{post}} , because it releases intermediate checkpoints along both its pretraining and post-training trajectories, which lets us vary θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} rather than fix it to the official base model. Math data We consider three settings for where the off-policy data comes from (see § A ): • Distillation with teacher traces : we get teacher traces from the AoPS subset of Nemotron-SFT-Math-v4 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ; Du et al., 2025 ) , whose solutions are generated by DeepSeek-V4-Pro ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) . At both scales we mine hard problems from this pool that the post-trained model cannot solve. For each model, we sample 16 16 attempts per problem and keep those with 0 0 success for 1.7B and ≤ 1 \leq 1 success for 8B, leaving 1,533 1{,}533 training samples for 1.7B and 985 985 for 8B. • Self-improvement with rejection sampling (STaR; Zelikman et al., 2022 ): we apply rejection sampling to the post-trained model to get supervision of both thinking and solution tokens. We sample up to 32 32 attempts per problem and keep one verified trace for each solved problem. • Self-improvement with Pedagogical RL ( Chakraborty et al., 2026 ) : STaR requires that the model can solve the problem with a large budget. Pedagogical RL removes this requirement by synthesizing reasoning traces from gold solutions and do SFT on the synthesized traces (Appendix B ). We find replacing the SFT step of Pedagogical RL with grafting largely improves performance. Evaluation For math, new-task performance is measured on around 100 100 held-out hard math problems from the training set. Old-task performance is the mean over three benchmarks (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, HMMT 2025). All metrics are estimated over 16 16 samples at temperature 1.0 1.0 and top- p p 1.0 1.0 , decoding up to 32 32 K tokens in thinking mode, unless otherwise specified. Appendix C gives the training details.

sections.heading: 5.2 Model merging alone improves both old and new tasks
sections.text: We first show that model merging already improves both old and new tasks. We consider three methods: SFT, OPSD, and grafting, with full details given in Appendix C . In Figure 2 , we sweep all methods with 9 9 learning rates ( 5 × 10 − 7 5{\times}10^{-7} to 5 × 10 − 5 5{\times}10^{-5} ) and train 5 5 epochs. Figure 2 (left) shows that, without model merging, neither SFT nor OPSD outperforms the post-trained model, while grafting with the best hyperparameters does. We then sweep the merging scale for all methods in Figure 2 (right). We see that merging improves generalization and erases OPSD’s original edge over SFT, despite its slow and expensive on-policy sampling. Given its uniform benefit, we apply merging across all methods in the rest of the paper. Figure 2: Model merging improves both old and new task performance.

sections.heading: 5.3 Optimal θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} is before the end of pretraining
sections.text: OLMo-3-7B (thinking) ( OLMo Team, 2026 ) has many checkpoints for us to move θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} freely. On the post-training side, we have base model → SFT \xrightarrow{\text{SFT}} SFT checkpoint → DPO \xrightarrow{\text{DPO}} DPO checkpoint → RL \xrightarrow{\text{RL}} OLMo-3-7B (thinking); on the pretraining side, we move θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} up to 12 12 k steps before the base model. We first investigate how each post-training stage makes finetuning harder. We see in Figure 3 (left) that grafting (base ckpt) outperforms grafting (SFT ckpt), grafting (SFT ckpt) outperforms grafting (DPO ckpt), and grafting (DPO ckpt) outperforms direct SFT on the final post-trained model. This suggests that each stage of post-training (SFT, DPO, RL) makes OLMo-3 harder to finetune. The question that remains is which pretraining checkpoint to use as the donor model. There is a tension in this choice. The end of pretraining anneals on higher-quality data and already resembles an early stage of SFT, so an earlier θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} should be easier to finetune, but it also sits farther from θ post \theta_{\text{post}} , which makes it less likely to stay linearly connected ( Frankle et al., 2020 ; Neyshabur et al., 2020 ) with θ post \theta_{\text{post}} . Figure 3 (right) moves θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} up to 12 12 k steps before the final base checkpoint. We see that earlier pretrained checkpoints clearly outperforms the final pretrained checkpoint, while the gain is not strictly monotonic. This suggests that for grafting we should search for an early pretrained checkpoint that balances the two forces. Qwen3 releases only its final base model and no earlier pretraining checkpoints, so in the rest of the paper we use the official base model as θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} . sections.heading: 5.4 Results for distillation with teacher traces
sections.text: Thinking mode Figure 4(a) and Figure 4(b) show results with teacher traces as off-policy data, on Qwen3-1.7B (thinking) and Qwen3-8B (thinking), respectively. The same merging sweep (§ 5.2 ) is applied for all methods. We see that, for 1.7B, grafting dominates both SFT and OPSD and is the only method that meaningfully dominates the post-trained model. The same ordering holds at pass@4 and pass@8, suggesting that the gain reflects expanded capability and not simply a “sharpening effect”. For 8B, both grafting and SFT dominate OPSD. For both sizes, OPSD fails to largely outperform the original post-trained model for generalization, which echoes the findings in Kim et al. (2026) ; Kaur et al. (2026) . Non-thinking mode (aka. instruct mode) We repeat the experiment at 8B in non-thinking mode on DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , an easier data for the non-thinking mode to learn, and we follow the thinking mode experiments to mine hard problems (see Appendix A for details). The same merging sweep (§ 5.2 ) is applied for all methods. We see from Figure 4(c) that grafting again dominates SFT and OPSD at pass@ 1 1 .

sections.heading: 5.5 Self-improvement with rejection sampling (STaR)
sections.text: Figure 5: Self-improvement with rejection sampling (STaR) on Qwen3-1.7B (thinking). We now turn to the second setting, where the off-policy data come from the post-trained model itself via rejection sampling (§ 5.1 ), also known as STaR ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) . Specifically, we sample up to 32 32 attempts per problem and keep one verified trace for each solved problem. Unlike distillation from teacher traces, STaR lets the model self-improve by training on its own data. Figure 5 shows that new-task performance is roughly the same compared to the strongest baseline (i.e., SFT, which stands for the original STaR) but generalization to old task rises about eight points above it. Compared to distillation from teacher traces (Figure 4(a) ), we see that STaR is generally worse in terms of new-task performance but similar for generalization to the old task.

sections.heading: 5.6 Self-improvement with Pedagogical RL
sections.text: Figure 6: Self-improvement with Pedagogical RL on Qwen3-1.7B (thinking). Pedagogical RL ( Chakraborty et al., 2026 ) takes a different route to self-improvement, where a copy of the model that sees the reference solution (without seeing thinking traces) is trained with RL to write thinking traces the model can learn from (Appendix B ). With these self-generated thinking traces, the original method then learns with SFT (Pedagogical RL + SFT in Figure 6 ). Compared to direct distillation from teacher traces, Pedagogical RL does not need access to thinking traces, which is more practical since solutions from humans or expert systems do not expose thinking traces. We keep the RL training and thinking trace generation steps intact and propose to learn the same traces with grafting. Since Pedagogical RL is designed to generate thinking traces and OPSD does not use them, we reuse the OPSD results from STaR (§ 5.5 ). Figure 6 shows that grafting again dominates SFT and OPSD. With Pedagogical RL, grafting learns the new task better and generalizes to the old task, while SFT loses in both directions.

sections.heading: 6.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: Models We experiment with Qwen3-1.7B (thinking) as the post-trained model θ post \theta_{\text{post}} and Qwen3-1.7B-Base Yang et al. (2025) as the donor model θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} . Knowledge data Our data for knowledge acquisition mainly follows Shenfeld et al. (2026) , but with the key exception that we use purely synthetic knowledge to avoid any possible leakage. We construct a fictional world with 200 200 invented entities and 1,125 1{,}125 atomic facts. Each fact is written as question-answer pairs in 8 8 distinct phrasings, and the model is trained on those; evaluation then uses held-out paraphrases the model has never seen. For OPSD, we write wiki-style articles that state the fictional facts for conditioning. Since the knowledge data’s QA form is very different from a reasoning model’s, we mix knowledge QA with AoPS teacher traces we use in the math experiments. Together, we have 9,000 9{,}000 QA samples and 1,533 1{,}533 AoPS traces. All methods are trained on this same mixture. Evaluation For knowledge, new-task performance is the exact-match accuracy on held-out paraphrases the model never saw, decoded greedily. Old-task performance is the mean over three benchmarks (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, HMMT 2025). Appendix C gives the training details. Figure 7: (Left) Knowledge injection results. (Right) Disentangling the contribution of grafting’s components. The protection mask ( ρ \rho sweep) dominates no mask ( λ \lambda sweep).

sections.heading: 6.2 Knowledge injection results
sections.text: Figure 7 (left) shows the knowledge injection result with Qwen3-1.7B (thinking), where the same model merging sweep (§ 5.2 ) is applied to all methods. We see that grafting achieves nearly perfect injection with retention at or above the post-trained model. SFT injects just as well but suffers from forgetting. OPSD achieves near-perfect retention but also learns less. Within OPSD, forward KL ( α = 0 \alpha{=}0 ) learns much more than JSD ( α = 0.5 \alpha{=}0.5 ) and reverse KL ( α = 1 \alpha{=}1 ). This shows that learning a new fact requires a mode-covering objective rather than mode-seeking.

sections.heading: 7  Analysis
sections.text: Ablation studies Here we ablate the mask step that zeroes the most sensitive coordinates. Figure 7 (right) compares the protection mask ( ρ \rho sweep, in red) with plain model merging without the mask ( λ \lambda sweep, in gray). We see that the protection mask Pareto-dominates plain model merging. Figure 7 (right) also shows Fisher merging ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ) , which weights each coordinate by its Fisher ratio between the two tasks. We see that Fisher merging does not inject at all in this setting. We find that this is because the knowledge injection Fisher is usually dominated by the retention Fisher. Finally, the KFAC mask (§ 4 , in navy) reaches the same old-task performance as the diagonal mask while zeroing far fewer directions: at ρ = 0.001 \rho{=}0.001 it keeps new-task performance at 0.995 0.995 with old-task performance 0.390 0.390 , which the diagonal mask needs ρ = 0.01 \rho{=}0.01 to match. We note that KFAC being a better approximant to the retention Fisher does not directly imply interference must be more concentrated to few directions. The fact that retention of old tasks and injected knowledge can be achieved by zero-ing very few directions is in line with parallel work demonstrating the top few directions of curvature contain mostly interference ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and can be removed with little effect on task performance ( Song et al., 2025 ) . sections.heading: 8  Related Work
sections.text: Continual learning for post-trained models. Continually trained networks can overwrite earlier capabilities ( McCloskey and Cohen, 1989 ) . Classic remedies constrain the update written into the parameters, e.g., elastic weight consolidation ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ) . For language models, it has been shown that low-rank updates ( Hu et al., 2022 ) forget less but also learn less ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) . SFT and RL learn in different ways ( Chu et al., 2025 ; Matsutani et al., 2025 ) , and SFT in particular memorizes at the cost of generalization. This echoes the common belief is that continual training should be on-policy, and has been demonstrated by the success of continual training models using RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Chen et al. (2025) attribute RL’s smaller forgetting specifically to its use of on-policy data, rather than to other algorithmic choices such as KL regularization or advantage estimation. In practice, however, most data for continual learning is off-policy, such as knowledge after the pretraining cutoff ( Jang et al., 2022 ) , expert demonstrations ( Taori et al., 2023 ) , delayed feedback from environments ( Trajectory Labs, 2026 ) , and synthetic data for self-improvement Zelikman et al. (2022) . On-policy self-distillation and its failure modes. OPSD converts off-policy data into an on-policy learning signal, by distilling a solution-conditioned copy of the model into itself on its own samples ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hubotter et al., 2026 ; Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . The approach is being scaled in practice ( Trajectory Labs, 2026 ) . Its benefit, however, appears to hold only within a limited scope of tasks. Reported failure modes include suppressed exploration, degeneration in reasoning length, and failure to generalize ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Kaur et al., 2026 ) . Recent work responds to these failures by filtering the part of the teacher signal that does not transfer to the student ( Shen et al., 2026 ) or by routing token-level supervision between privileged teacher and student policies ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Model merging and weight-space operations. Weight-space operations are promised by loss-landscape geometry ( Frankle et al., 2020 ; Neyshabur et al., 2020 ; Ainsworth et al., 2023 ) , and a large literature does weight interpolation with models trained or finetuned with the same initialization ( Wortsman et al., 2022a ; Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Wortsman et al., 2022b ; Ilharco et al., 2022 ) , with refinements that resolve interference, linearize fine-tuning, or localize a skill in a sparse subset of the delta ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Ortiz-Jimenez et al., 2023 ; Panigrahi et al., 2023 ) . Model merging has been shown to improve robustness ( Wortsman et al., 2022b ) and generation diversity ( Dang et al., 2025 ) . Most similar to our work, task arithmetic Ilharco et al. (2023) , also known as Shadow-FT ( Wu et al., 2025 ) or chat vector Huang et al. (2024) , composes weight deltas trained on the base model. We improve over them with the proposed Fisher masking and donor model selection. Fisher merging ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ) derives a soft weighting between multiple tasks that train the model, while we derive a sparse mask using only the retention data and show that retention-only sparse masking is substantially more effective. Models become harder to finetune. It has been known that training changes how well a model takes a further update, or plasticity ( Ash and Adams, 2020 ; Dohare et al., 2024 ) . Recent work demonstrates this for large language models. The longer a base model is pretrained beyond a certain point, the more sensitive its parameters become and the worse it finetunes ( Springer et al., 2025 ) . To mitigate such overtraining effect, it has been proposed to increase learning rate ( Rofin et al., 2026 ) , or more broadly, to bias pretraining toward flatter minima ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . Our experiments on varying the donor model for grafting point the same way: an earlier pretraining checkpoint can be a better θ donor \theta_{\text{donor}} than the final base model and later post-trained intermediate checkpoints. Different from previous work, we show that the harder-to-finetune effect can be mitigated not only by training an easier-to-finetune model, but also by better continual update rules.

sections.heading: 9  Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We asked whether continual learning for RL-trained models has to be on-policy, and our results suggest that it does not. Model merging alone shows that SFT learns a useful signal from new data, but naively applying its update interferes with existing capabilities. Building on that, grafting reduces this interference by learning the update on an earlier donor checkpoint, scaling it, and optionally masking the most sensitive update directions. Across three settings, grafting Pareto-dominates both SFT and OPSD in new-task and old-task performance, while avoiding expensive on-policy sampling. We show that w donor model to use for grafting turns out to be crucial too. Earlier pretraining checkpoints are usually a better choice, though future work can study more principled approaches to select the optimal pretraining checkpoint for grafting. Another direction to optimize for future work is to predict optimal λ \lambda and ρ \rho instead of a sweep. More broadly, since off-policy data is what continual learning mostly has, we hope this work encourages more effort on making off-policy training generalize.

sections.text: Knowledge (synthetic closed world). To guarantee the facts are new, we build a closed fictional world rather than reuse public corpora: 200 200 invented entities and 1,125 1{,}125 atomic facts about them. For OPSD we additionally write 200 200 wiki-style articles that state the facts, used only for conditioning. The facts are absent from the post-trained model: closed-book exact-match is ≈ 0 % \approx\!0\% (instruct 0.09 % 0.09\% , base 0.13 % 0.13\% ). Answers are scored by rule-based <answer> exact-match. All methods train on the same mixture of the 9,000 9{,}000 QA pairs and the 1,533 1{,}533 AoPS traces of the math corpus. Math reasoning, Qwen3-1.7B (thinking). Training traces are competition math solutions sampled from the AoPS split of Nemotron-SFT-Math [ NVIDIA, 2026 ] . We mine the hard subset by sampling Qwen3-1.7B (thinking) 16 16 times per problem at temperature 1.0 1.0 and keeping only problems it fails on all 16 16 attempts, so the target skill is absent. After length-filtering and deduplication we keep 1,533 1{,}533 training traces, and hold out a disjoint set of 111 111 mined-hard problems to measure new-task performance. On post-trained models, supervised finetuning (SFT) on new data often causes poor generalization and catastrophic forgetting. As such, the conventional wisdom is that on-policy training is a prerequisite for continual learning. In practice, however, data containing new knowledge or capabilities are often off-policy . While methods such as on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) try to bridge this gap by converting off-policy data into on-policy signal, they have been shown to cause reasoning collapse. In this paper, we show that off-policy merging beats OPSD for continual learning . We first show that SFT learns a useful signal from new data, but naively applying its update interferes with existing capabilities. We reduce this interference with a simple recipe we term grafting , which changes where the update is learned and how it is applied: (1) learning the update on an earlier donor checkpoint , ideally even before the end of pretraining , and applying the weight update to the post-trained model; (2) scaling the weight update, equivalent to a form of model merging; and (3) optionally, masking the most sensitive update directions when the new data distribution is far from the post-trained model. Across continual learning settings including (1) distilling from expert traces, (2) self-improvement with STaR and Pedagogical RL, and (3) injecting knowledge after pretraining cutoff, grafting Pareto-dominates both SFT and OPSD in new-task and old-task performance, while avoiding expensive on-policy sampling. Therefore, our work challenges on-policy training as a necessity for continual learning on RL-trained models. This is particularly challenging for models that have undergone extensive post-training. In particular, direct supervised finetuning (SFT) on new data can cause forgetting and fail to generalize ( Chu et al., 2025 ) . This has motivated the view that continual learning should remain on-policy , i.e. the model learns from behavior produced by its current policy ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . However, extended on-policy RL can plateau and lose coverage after exhausting non-zero reward behaviors to amplify ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Furthermore, data containing new knowledge or capabilities are often off-policy , such as new knowledge after the pretraining cutoff Jang et al. (2022) , expert demonstrations Taori et al. (2023) , delayed feedback from environments Trajectory Labs (2026) , and synthetic data for self-improvement Chakraborty et al. (2026) . Recent work on on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) tries to bridge this gap by converting off-policy data into on-policy updates, distilling from a solution-conditioned copy of the model ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Hubotter et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . However, conditioning on the solution can suppress exploration, leak privileged information into the teacher’s reasoning, and degrade out-of-domain performance or collapse reasoning length ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Kaur et al., 2026 ) . More fundamentally, this raises a simple question: Is on-policy training necessary for continual learning, or are we using off-policy updates poorly? A task may be a skill (e.g., a class of hard math problems) or some knowledge (e.g., new facts after the knowledge cutoff). Two objectives should be optimized jointly: • New task : performance on held-out IID instances of the target task. • Old task : performance on tasks outside the target task – for unrelated tasks, we want less forgetting; for related tasks, we want the new skill or knowledge to generalize to these tasks. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a standard way to learn a task without using off-policy data. For genuinely new knowledge or very hard problems beyond the model’s capability, the model places almost no probability on correct outputs and, therefore, receives no training signal to continue improving. These are the scenarios where off-policy data can be extremely useful. Continually trained networks can overwrite earlier capabilities ( McCloskey and Cohen, 1989 ) . Classic remedies constrain the update written into the parameters, e.g., elastic weight consolidation ( Kirkpatrick et al., 2017 ) . For language models, it has been shown that low-rank updates ( Hu et al., 2022 ) forget less but also learn less ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) . SFT and RL learn in different ways ( Chu et al., 2025 ; Matsutani et al., 2025 ) , and SFT in particular memorizes at the cost of generalization. This echoes the common belief is that continual training should be on-policy, and has been demonstrated by the success of continual training models using RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Chen et al. (2025) attribute RL’s smaller forgetting specifically to its use of on-policy data, rather than to other algorithmic choices such as KL regularization or advantage estimation. In practice, however, most data for continual learning is off-policy, such as knowledge after the pretraining cutoff ( Jang et al., 2022 ) , expert demonstrations ( Taori et al., 2023 ) , delayed feedback from environments ( Trajectory Labs, 2026 ) , and synthetic data for self-improvement Zelikman et al. (2022) . On-policy self-distillation and its failure modes. OPSD converts off-policy data into an on-policy learning signal, by distilling a solution-conditioned copy of the model into itself on its own samples ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Hubotter et al., 2026 ; Penaloza et al., 2026 ) . The approach is being scaled in practice ( Trajectory Labs, 2026 ) . Its benefit, however, appears to hold only within a limited scope of tasks. Reported failure modes include suppressed exploration, degeneration in reasoning length, and failure to generalize ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Kaur et al., 2026 ) . Recent work responds to these failures by filtering the part of the teacher signal that does not transfer to the student ( Shen et al., 2026 ) or by routing token-level supervision between privileged teacher and student policies ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . Model merging and weight-space operations. Weight-space operations are promised by loss-landscape geometry ( Frankle et al., 2020 ; Neyshabur et al., 2020 ; Ainsworth et al., 2023 ) , and a large literature does weight interpolation with models trained or finetuned with the same initialization ( Wortsman et al., 2022a ; Matena and Raffel, 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Wortsman et al., 2022b ; Ilharco et al., 2022 ) , with refinements that resolve interference, linearize fine-tuning, or localize a skill in a sparse subset of the delta ( Yadav et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2024 ; Ortiz-Jimenez et al., 2023 ; Panigrahi et al., 2023 ) . Model merging has been shown to improve robustness ( Wortsman et al., 2022b ) and generation diversity ( Dang et al., 2025 ) . Most similar to our work, task arithmetic Ilharco et al. (2023) , also known as Shadow-FT ( Wu et al., 2025 ) or chat vector Huang et al. (2024) , composes weight deltas trained on the base model. We improve over them with the proposed Fisher masking and donor model selection. Fisher merging ( Matena and Raffel, 2022 ) derives a soft weighting between multiple tasks that train the model, while we derive a sparse mask using only the retention data and show that retention-only sparse masking is substantially more effective. Models become harder to finetune. It has been known that training changes how well a model takes a further update, or plasticity ( Ash and Adams, 2020 ; Dohare et al., 2024 ) . Recent work demonstrates this for large language models. The longer a base model is pretrained beyond a certain point, the more sensitive its parameters become and the worse it finetunes ( Springer et al., 2025 ) . To mitigate such overtraining effect, it has been proposed to increase learning rate ( Rofin et al., 2026 ) , or more broadly, to bias pretraining toward flatter minima ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . Our experiments on varying the donor model for grafting point the same way: an earlier pretraining checkpoint can be a better θ donor 	heta_{	ext{donor}} than the final base model and later post-trained intermediate checkpoints. Different from previous work, we show that the harder-to-finetune effect can be mitigated not only by training an easier-to-finetune model, but also by better continual update rules. 9 Conclusion and Future Work We asked whether continual learning for RL-trained models has to be on-policy, and our results suggest that it does not. Model merging alone shows that SFT learns a useful signal from new data, but naively applying its update interferes with existing capabilities. Building on that, grafting reduces this interference by learning the update on an earlier donor checkpoint, scaling it, and optionally masking the most sensitive update directions. Across three settings, grafting Pareto-dominates both SFT and OPSD in new-task and old-task performance, while avoiding expensive on-policy sampling. We show that w donor model to use for grafting turns out to be crucial too. Earlier pretraining checkpoints are usually a better choice, though future work can study more principled approaches to select the optimal pretraining checkpoint for grafting. Another direction to optimize for future work is to predict optimal λ \lambda and ρ ho instead of a sweep. More broadly, since off-policy data is what continual learning mostly has, we hope this work encourages more effort on making off-policy training generalize.
